ta-l1d34q2-d1e100.summary: The second question of Distinction 34 asks about the appropriation in the text (power to the Father, wisdom to the Son, goodness to the Spirit), with a first argument that it is unfitting: virtue pertains to power, and virtue is appropriated to the Son (1 Cor. 1:24, 'Christ the power of God'), so power should be the Son's.
claims: Virtus is appropriated to the Son.

ta-l1d34q2-d1e106.summary: Second argument. Wisdom is the principle of uttering the Word, and speaking the Word belongs to the Father, its principle, so wisdom should be appropriated to the Father.
claims: Wisdom is the principle of the Word.

ta-l1d34q2-d1e109.summary: Third argument. The Son proceeds by way of nature as Son as well as by way of intellect as Word, so if wisdom is appropriated to him for the second, nature should be for the first.
claims: Nature should be appropriated to the Son.

ta-l1d34q2-d1e113.summary: Fourth argument. According to Dionysius the good is self-diffusive and quasi-fontal principle of every emanation of divine goodness, and being fontal principle belongs to the Father, so goodness should be his.

ta-l1d34q2-d1e119.summary: Thomas's determination. Personal names are said of God and creatures not univocally but by prior and posterior, so paternity and filiation are in creatures and in God in different ways, and appropriation can be made two ways: by the concepts of the names as said of creatures, and then it must be by contrast, to exclude the creaturely mode from the Creator; or by the concepts as found in God, and then by likeness to the proper (Dist. 31). Both ways the appropriation fits. By contrast: fathers among us are weak with age, so power is attributed to the heavenly Father; sons are unskilled from youthful impulse and inexperience, so wisdom is attributed to the Son of God; 'spirit' among us suggests rigidity, inflation, or impetuosity (Isa. 2:22, 'whose spirit is in his nostrils'), so goodness is attributed to the Holy Spirit, as the text notes. By likeness: power, which includes the character of principle (principle of change, Metaphysics 5), to the Father, fontal principle of all divinity; wisdom to the Son, who proceeds by way of intellect, perfected by wisdom; goodness to the Spirit, who proceeds by way of will, whose object is goodness.
claims: Appropriation works by contrast with creaturely defects or by likeness to divine propers.
By contrast: power against fathers' weakness, wisdom against sons' inexperience, goodness against 'spirit's' impetuosity.
By likeness: power to the principle, wisdom to the Word, goodness to Love.
concepts: appropriation by contrast and by likeness
personal names by prior and posterior

ta-l1d34q2-d1e125.summary: Reply to the first argument. Virtue names not power absolutely but its perfection, the utmost of a thing's power (the Philosopher). So it can be considered three ways: as rooted in power, appropriated to the Father like power; as that by which power goes into act, appropriated to the Son, through whom the Father acts, who is called the Father's arm (Job 40:4, as Gregory expounds); or as conferring goodness on the work (Ethics 2: virtue makes its possessor good and his work good), appropriated to the Spirit like goodness.
claims: Virtus can be appropriated to each person under a different aspect.
concepts: Son as arm of the Father

ta-l1d34q2-d1e131.summary: Reply to the second argument. Wisdom relates to the word as the same, as prior, or as posterior, in God as in humans. Our word, a conception of the intellect, follows an intellectual light, at least the agent intellect's and that of first principles from which a conclusion is drawn. Wisdom as knowledge of the conclusion is the same as the mental word; as the light of the agent intellect and knowledge of principles it precedes the word; as wisdom generated in a student by the master's word it follows the word. So in God begotten wisdom is the same as the Word (Dist. 32); the paternal intellect is like the agent intellect's light with principles in producing the Word, so by order of nature wisdom is principle of the Word, as unbegotten wisdom is principle of begotten wisdom; and created wisdom follows the Word as its effect (Sir. 1:5, 'the fountain of wisdom is the Word of God on high'). So essential wisdom, neither begotten nor begetting, can be appropriated to the Son by its likeness to his proper as Word, which it lacks to any proper of the Father.
claims: Wisdom is the same as, prior to, or posterior to the word in different senses.
Essential wisdom resembles the Son as Word, so it is appropriated to him.

ta-l1d34q2-d1e137.summary: Reply to the third argument. Nature always has the character of principle, the principle of motion and rest in that in which it is per se (Physics 2), so it cannot be appropriated to the Son, who is from a principle in the origin of nature and not principle in it. Wisdom has the character both of principle and of what is from a principle, more so since wisdom and knowledge properly concern conclusions, though wisdom also concerns principles (Ethics 6), so it can be appropriated to the Son.
claims: Nature is always a principle, so it is not appropriated to the Son; wisdom concerns conclusions too.

ta-l1d34q2-d1e141.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The good is called self-diffusive as end, as the end moves the agent, but the Father is principle of divinity rather as efficient.
claims: Goodness diffuses as end; the Father is principle as efficient.

ta-l1d34q2-Dd1e92.summary: The single article of the second question of Distinction 34 defends appropriating power to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and goodness to the Spirit, both by contrast, excluding creaturely defects (aged fathers' weakness, young sons' inexperience, the impetuosity of 'spirit'), and by likeness to the divine propers (principle, Word, Love). Virtue can be appropriated to each person under different aspects. Essential wisdom resembles the Son as Word. Nature, always a principle, is not appropriated to the Son, and goodness diffuses as end while the Father is principle as efficient.
claims: Power, wisdom, and goodness are appropriated by contrast with creatures and by likeness to the propers.

ta-l1d34q2.summary: Quaestio 2 of Book I, Distinction 34 defends the appropriation of power to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and goodness to the Spirit. Appropriation works by contrast, excluding creaturely defects of fathers, sons, and 'spirit', and by likeness to the divine propers. Replies show how virtue, wisdom, nature, and goodness fit or do not fit each person.
claims: Appropriations work by contrast with creatures and by likeness to the persons' propers.
